en: Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, a newly ordained monk who is endowed with virtue and other such qualities, and who desires to quickly destroy passion, hatred, and delusion, should frequently visit a cemetery. Having gone to the cemetery, he should approach the corpses."

Having approached corpses, one should grasp the sign—namely, the sign of a corpse that is bluish-black, or festering, or worm-eaten, or bloated, or devoured by animals, or bloody, or scattered, or a skeleton, or a chain of bones, or a heap of bones. Having grasped the sign, one should return to one’s lodgings with all possible haste.

Having come to his lodging and washed his feet outside the monastery, he should enter the monastery and sit down on a couch, or on a grass mat, or on a bench. Having sat down on that very couch, or on the grass mat, or on the bench, that monk should cultivate that same perception.

That is to say, having grasped the sign—whether it be a livid corpse, or a festering corpse, or a worm-infested corpse, or a bloated corpse, or a devoured corpse, or a blood-stained corpse, or a scattered corpse, or bones, or a skeleton, or a chain of bones—the monk should cultivate that very perception. By quickly fading away from passion, hatred, and ignorance, and by generating true knowledge, the monk shall attain the destruction of suffering.
The Blessed One said this; having spoken thus, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
"If a novice monk who is still in training has not yet attained his goal, he should go to the cemetery if he desires to destroy passion. (1)
With a mind free from malice and compassionate toward all beings,
he should pervade all directions and then approach his own bodies.
If he should see a livid corpse, or if he should see one festering with pus; if he should see a bloated corpse, or even a skeleton of bones. (3)
Cultivating that very perception, he should go to his place of rest. Having reached his place of rest and having washed his feet with mindfulness,
he should sit down upon a couch, or on a grass mat, or else upon a small stool.
Then, having sat down upon a couch, or on a grass mat, or even on a stool,
one should examine one's own body— above, within, and likewise without.
It is full of feces, urine, kidneys, and the heart.
Of the liver, fat, and marrow, and also of the small and large intestines. || 6 ||
If he should go for a meal, or go into a village for alms,
he should always be well-armored, with mindfulness as his forerunner, like a warrior.
Having seen a beautiful and pleasing form associated with passion, one should cultivate the perception of the foul there, being single-minded and well-composed. (8)
From this [body], there is nothing at all to be taken—neither bone, nor flesh, nor even blood;
neither liver, nor lungs, nor marrow, nor spleen, nor brain. (9)
The earth element is purposeless, and the water element is purposeless;
the fire element is purposeless, and the wind element is purposeless. (10)
And whatever pleasant feelings exist here that are accompanied by passion, their subsiding occurs when one perceives them with wisdom. (11)
Dwelling thus, ardent and untiring day and night,
quickly causing the fading away of passion, hatred, and ignorance,
and generating true knowledge, the monk shall attain the destruction of suffering. (12)
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
